57.title: The well
57.hook: they drop him into a well, and Allah inspires him that one day he'll tell them what they did
57.carry: even in the well, a promise
57.tomorrow: The shirt and the false blood
57.howItsDone: Muslims often recite and reflect on Surah Yusuf in times of grief or hardship; the promise to Yusuf in the well is remembered as a sign that Allah reaches people where no one else can.

screen: `DAY FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the brothers' plan, jealousy with repentance already scheduled. Your line was jealousy makes plans. Did you catch one, and name it? Day fifty-seven.
screen: `JEALOUSY MAKES PLANS.`

segments.voice: The brothers have their plan. Now they need their father to let the boy go. So they go to Ya'qub, all warmth. Father, why don't you trust us with Yusuf? We only wish him well. Send him with us tomorrow. He'll run and play, and we'll look after him. And Ya'qub says something that should chill them. It grieves me that you'd take him away. And I'm afraid a wolf might eat him while you're not paying attention. A wolf. He's handed them the words. They answer: if a wolf eats him, with all of us there, we'd be losers indeed. And in the morning, the boy goes out with them. Today: the well.
screen: `FATHER, TRUST US WITH HIM.` → `I FEAR A WOLF.` → `HE GOES WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse fifteen, and the Qur'an tells the worst moment in almost no words. So when they took him away, and agreed to put him in the depths of the well. That's it. No description of the struggle, the shouting, the boy's face. The Qur'an doesn't linger on the cruelty. It moves straight to what matters more. And We inspired him: you will surely tell them about this deed of theirs, while they do not realize. Picture where that promise lands. A boy, maybe still a child, at the bottom of a dark, damp well, his brothers' voices fading overhead. And into that darkness comes a message: this isn't the end. One day you'll stand in front of them and tell them what they did, and they won't even know who you are. It doesn't take him out of the well. It doesn't stop the caravan, or the slavery, or the prison that's coming. It gives him a thread to hold in the dark. Notice who the promise is for. Not the brothers; they don't hear it. Not Ya'qub; he's at home, waiting. Just Yusuf, alone, where nobody else can reach. The Arabic for the depths of the well is ghayabat al-jubb. Ghayaba comes from the root for what's hidden, unseen, the same root as al-ghayb, the unseen world that Muslims believe in. The bottom of the well is the place where you vanish from sight. And that's exactly where the promise reaches him. Some years later, and a few days from now for us, we'll see it kept.
screen: `THE WORST, IN A FEW WORDS.` · `YOU WILL SURELY TELL THEM.` · `A THREAD TO HOLD IN THE DARK.` · `GHAYABAT — THE HIDDEN DEPTHS.` · then, large: `EVEN IN THE WELL, A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in a dark minute, not alone. If you can, close your eyes, or dim the light. Let the room get quiet. Think of the darkest place you've been, or are in now. You don't need to relive it. Just touch the edge of it. Then imagine that, even there, something reached you: a voice, a memory, a promise, a person. What was it? If nothing reached you then, imagine what you'd want to hear now. If you pray, you can remember that Allah reached Yusuf at the bottom of the well. The bell holds the time.
The well. Where Yusuf's brothers left him, and where a promise found him: one day you'll tell them what they did. Today's word.
screen: `THE WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: even in the well, a promise. If you know someone in a dark place today, be the voice that reaches them: one message, one call. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: The shirt and the false blood
58.hook: they bring his shirt with false blood, and Ya'qub says: beautiful patience
58.howItsDone: Muslims often say "sabrun jamil" to themselves or to one another in times of loss, recalling Ya'qub's words, and sabr is counted among the central virtues of faith.

screen: `DAY FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the well, and a promise that reached a boy in the dark. Your line was even in the well, a promise. Did you reach someone in a dark place? Day fifty-eight.
screen: `EVEN IN THE WELL, A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: It's evening. The brothers come home, and they're weeping. Loudly. Father, we went off racing each other, and we left Yusuf by our things, and a wolf ate him. And then, before he's said a word, they add: but you won't believe us, even though we're telling the truth. When someone tells you they're telling the truth before you've asked, you already know. And they have evidence. They hold up his shirt, stained with blood. Not his blood. The Qur'an calls it false blood. Every parent has a nightmare, and this is the one. Today's word is what Ya'qub says next.
screen: `EVENING. THE BROTHERS WEEP.` → `A WOLF ATE HIM.` → `A SHIRT, WITH FALSE BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Ya'qub looks at the shirt. Commentators have long pointed out a detail: a wolf that eats a boy but leaves his shirt without a tear? And he says: no. Your own selves have talked you into something. And then two words, in Arabic, sabrun jamil. Pickthall's old translation renders it "comely patience." Beautiful patience. Sabr: patience, endurance, holding steady. Jamil: beautiful. It isn't gritted-teeth patience, the kind that sighs loudly and tells everyone how much it's suffering. Muslim scholars have explained sabr jamil as patience without complaint to people. You can still grieve. You just don't turn the grief into a weapon against those around you. And he adds: and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe. He knows they're lying. He doesn't scream. He doesn't beat it out of them. He doesn't pretend to believe them either. He names it, and then he waits. Now, the mistake to avoid: sabr jamil doesn't mean feeling nothing. Later in this very surah, Ya'qub weeps for Yusuf until his eyes turn white with grief. And when his sons tell him he'll grieve himself to death, he says: I only complain of my sorrow and grief to Allah. That's the shape of it. The tears are real. The complaint goes up, not out. Beautiful patience is a way of carrying pain, not a way of not having it. Ya'qub will carry this for years. He says those two words again, later, when a second son is lost.
screen: `A WOLF, AND NO TEAR?` · `YOUR SELVES TALKED YOU INTO IT.` · `PATIENCE WITHOUT COMPLAINT.` · `THE COMPLAINT GOES UP, NOT OUT.` · then, large: `SABRUN JAMIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one hurt without complaining to anyone. Settle, and breathe. Find something that's hurting right now. A slight, an unfairness, a loss. Notice the part of you that wants to tell someone, to vent, to get the story out and get it agreed with. You don't have to shut the feeling down. Let it be there. Just, for these two minutes, and maybe for today, don't hand it to anyone. If you pray, you can do what Ya'qub did, and tell it to Allah instead. If you don't, just hold it, gently, like something fragile. And if something is truly harming you, telling someone who can help isn't complaining; that's wisdom. The bell holds the time.
Sabr jamil. Beautiful patience: grief that's real, carried without turning it on the people around you. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: beautiful patience. Carry one hurt today without venting it, and see what it feels like by evening. Day fifty-eight.

59.title: Sold for a few coins
59.hook: a caravan pulls him out and sells him cheaply in Egypt
59.carry: the price they paid isn't your worth
59.howItsDone: Muslims often draw from Yusuf's sale the teaching that human judgments of worth are not Allah's, and recite 12:21 ("Allah is in full command of His affairs") in times of setback.

screen: `DAY FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabr jamil, and a father who named the lie and then waited. Your line was beautiful patience. Did you carry one hurt without venting it? Day fifty-nine.
screen: `BEAUTIFUL PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Back to the well. A caravan of travelers comes by, the kind that crossed that land for centuries, camels loaded, heading for Egypt. They're thirsty. They send their water-drawer to the well, and he lets down his bucket. And it comes up heavy. He looks in and shouts: good news! Here's a boy! Think about what that means to a boy who's been waiting in the dark. Rescue, finally. Except the men up top aren't rescuers. They're traders. And a boy, to a trader, is something else. Today: sold for a few coins.
screen: `A CARAVAN, THIRSTY.` → `THE BUCKET COMES UP HEAVY.` → `GOOD NEWS! A BOY!`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. They hid him away as merchandise. And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, counted out. The Arabic for that price is bakhs, a cheated, short-changed price, less than a thing is worth. And the verse adds: they thought little of him. The boy who dreamed the stars bowing, sold for pocket change by men who didn't much care. Commentators have noted that a price you can count, a few coins rather than a weighed amount, was itself a sign of how cheap it was. But now watch the next verse, because the Qur'an turns the whole scene around. The man in Egypt who bought him says to his wife: make his stay honorable. Perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son. Does that sound familiar? It should. Two weeks ago, in Pharaoh's palace, Asiya looked at baby Musa and said almost the same words: perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son. Two boys, in two stories, taken into an Egyptian house by someone who saw what the world had missed. And then the verse says: and so We established Yusuf in the land, and Allah is in full command of His affairs, but most people don't know. The traders set the price. They didn't set his worth. The same boy they sold for a handful of coins is, in the story's own words, being established. Nobody watching that sale could have guessed it. That's the point.
screen: `HIDDEN AS MERCHANDISE.` · `BAKHS — A SHORT-CHANGED PRICE.` · `MAKE HIS STAY HONORABLE.` · `ESTABLISHED IN THE LAND.` · then, large: `THE PRICE ISN'T THE WORTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you've been undervalued. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone set a low price on you. Passed over for the job. Talked over in the meeting. Treated like you were extra in your own family. Let it come up, honestly. Then, gently, separate two things. What they paid, or thought, or offered. And what you actually are. Say it to yourself slowly: that was their price, not my worth. If you pray, you can remember that the Qur'an says most people don't know how things will turn. The bell holds the time.
Sold for a few coins. Yusuf, pulled from the well and sold cheap in Egypt, by men who thought little of him. Today's word.
screen: `SOLD FOR A FEW COINS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the price they paid isn't your worth. When someone underrates you today, or you underrate someone else, remember the caravan. Day fifty-nine.

60.title: The house of the Aziz
60.hook: the lady of the house tries to seduce him, and he says: I seek refuge in Allah
60.howItsDone: Muslims say a'udhu billah, "I seek refuge in Allah," before reciting the Qur'an, when angry, and when tempted; Yusuf's words in the house of the Aziz are a well-known example.

screen: `DAY SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sold for a few coins, and a boy the traders thought little of. Your line was the price they paid isn't your worth. Did you catch a low price on anyone? Day sixty.
screen: `THE PRICE THEY PAID ISN'T YOUR WORTH.`

segments.voice: Temptation rarely arrives when you're weak and alone in a dark alley. More often it shows up when life is finally going well. You've got the job, the trust, the key to the building. Nobody's watching. Yusuf has grown up in the house of the man who bought him. The Qur'an calls that man al-Aziz, a title, something like the great one, a high official of Egypt. Yusuf has reached his full strength, and the verse says he's been given wisdom and knowledge. He's trusted, he's handsome, he lives under their roof. And the lady of the house has noticed. Today: the house of the Aziz.
screen: `TEMPTATION WHEN THINGS GO WELL.` → `AL-AZIZ, A HIGH OFFICIAL.` → `THE LADY OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse twenty-three, told with great restraint. She, in whose house he was, tried to turn him from himself. She closed the doors, and said: come. And Yusuf's answer, in Pickthall's old translation: "I seek refuge in Allah!" In Arabic, ma'adha-llah. Then he gives his reasons: he's my master, he's treated me well; and wrongdoers don't prosper. Who does he mean by my master? Commentators split. Some say the Aziz, the man who gave him a good home. Others say his Lord, Allah. The Arabic word, rabb, can carry both, and the verse may be holding both at once: loyalty to the man who trusted him, and to the God who made him. Then comes a verse scholars have discussed for centuries: she desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the clear sign of his Lord. What was the sign? The Qur'an doesn't say. Commentators have offered many answers; the text stays silent. What it does say is that Yusuf was human, the pull was real, and he turned. That phrase, I seek refuge in Allah, has a close cousin you'll hear everywhere in Muslim life: a'udhu billah. Muslims say it before reading the Qur'an, when anger rises, when a bad thought knocks. Seeking refuge is not proving you're strong. It's admitting you need a place to run to, and running there. Yusuf didn't argue with the temptation, or try to out-think it. He named where he was going, and he went.
screen: `SHE CLOSED THE DOORS.` · `I SEEK REFUGE IN ALLAH!` · `MY MASTER — THE MAN, OR GOD?` · `THE SIGN OF HIS LORD.` · then, large: `A'UDHU BILLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your refuge before the knock. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing that tempts you most often. It might be small: the extra drink, the cruel comment, the scroll at two in the morning, the lie that would make things easier. Picture it knocking. Now, instead of arguing with it, picture turning and walking to somewhere safe. If you pray, you can say a'udhu billah, I seek refuge in Allah, and let the words be the door you step through. If not, choose one word that means safe to you, and practice going there. The bell holds the time.
The house of the Aziz. Where Yusuf, trusted and tempted behind closed doors, said: I seek refuge in Allah. Today's word.

61.title: Torn from behind
61.hook: the shirt is torn from the back, and a witness says that proves who ran
61.howItsDone: Muslims often point to the torn shirt as an example of Allah bringing the truth to light, and to Yusuf's calm answer as the way to respond when falsely accused.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the house of the Aziz, and a young man who ran to refuge. Your line was I seek refuge. Did you turn toward it once when something knocked? Day sixty-one.
screen: `I SEEK REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Yusuf said I seek refuge in Allah, and then he did the most practical thing a person can do with temptation. He ran for the door. She ran after him. They both raced for it, the Qur'an says, and she caught hold of his shirt from behind, and it tore. And then the door opens, and there, standing in the doorway, is her husband. Everyone freezes. It's a moment straight out of a courtroom drama, except there's no courtroom and no lawyer. Just two stories, one husband, and a torn shirt. Today: torn from behind.
screen: `HE RUNS FOR THE DOOR.` → `SHE CATCHES HIS SHIRT.` → `THE HUSBAND IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. She speaks first, fast. What's the penalty for someone who meant harm to your wife, except prison or a painful punishment? She doesn't even say what he did. She jumps to the sentence. Yusuf answers simply: she tried to turn me from myself. That's all. And then a witness from her own family speaks. The Qur'an says only a witness of her household; who it was, the text doesn't say. Some commentators report it was a wise man of her family; others tell a story that it was an infant who spoke. The witness says: look at the shirt. If it's torn from the front, she's telling the truth and he's lying. If it's torn from the back, she's lying and he's telling the truth. It's simple, almost like a detective's rule. Someone lunging at you tears the front. Someone running from you gets caught from behind. The husband looks. Torn from behind. And he says: this is your scheming, and turns to Yusuf: leave this alone. And to his wife: ask forgiveness for your wrong. Notice what Yusuf did not do. He didn't give a speech. He didn't attack her. He said one true sentence and let the evidence speak. And this is the second shirt in the surah. The first came home with false blood on it, and it lied. This one is torn from behind, and it tells the truth. There's one more shirt still to come in this story. Keep an eye on the shirts.
screen: `HER STORY COMES FIRST.` · `ONE TRUE SENTENCE.` · `A WITNESS: LOOK AT THE SHIRT.` · `THE SECOND SHIRT TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `TORN FROM BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the truth speak for itself once. Settle, and breathe. Think of a situation where you feel misunderstood, or accused, or where someone has the story wrong. Notice how much you want to explain, defend, send the long message, win. Now imagine saying one true, calm sentence, and stopping there. Just one. Let the facts, the shirt, do the rest. Say the sentence to yourself a few times, and feel what it's like not to add more. If you pray, you can ask for the truth to come out in its own time. The bell holds the time.
Torn from behind. The shirt that showed who ran and who chased, when Yusuf said one true sentence and stopped. Today's word.

62.title: The knives and the fruit
62.hook: the city's women, cutting fruit, see Yusuf and cut their hands
62.howItsDone: Muslims describe Yusuf as having been given great beauty, citing the hadith of the night journey, and read the banquet scene as a reminder that beauty, like wealth or power, is a trust and a test.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: torn from behind, a shirt that told the truth. Your line was the shirt tells. Did you say one true sentence and let it stand? Day sixty-two.
screen: `THE SHIRT TELLS.`

segments.voice: Some things you can't keep inside a house. The Aziz told everyone to leave it alone, and within days the whole city is talking. The Qur'an lets us hear the gossip. Women of the city are saying: the Aziz's wife is chasing her young servant. He's struck her heart with love. We think she's clearly lost her way. It's every whispered conversation at every party you've ever been to. And she hears about it. And she decides not to argue with the gossip. She's going to invite the gossips to dinner. Today: the knives and the fruit.
screen: `THE CITY IS TALKING.` → `STRUCK HER HEART WITH LOVE.` → `AN INVITATION TO DINNER.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. She sends for them, prepares a banquet with cushions to recline on, and gives each of them a knife. Then she tells Yusuf: come out to them. And when they see him, they're so struck that they cut their own hands. They say: Allah preserve us! This is no human being. This is nothing but a noble angel. And she says: there. That's the one you blamed me for. Now, the fruit. The title says fruit, and that's how the story is usually pictured, women peeling something when he walks in. But the Qur'an doesn't mention fruit at all. It mentions a banquet and knives. The fruit comes from the commentators, who wondered what the knives were for. Some said citrons; some said other things. The text is silent, and the image stuck anyway. The gossips' word for her love is worth a look too. They say shaghafaha hubban. Commentators explain shaghaf as the thin covering around the heart. Love had gone right through it. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, describing his night journey in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, said he met Yusuf, who had been given half of all beauty. So this story takes beauty seriously. It isn't sinful to be beautiful, and Yusuf did nothing here but walk into a room. But beauty tested everyone in that room. The women who mocked, and then couldn't hold a knife steady. The wife, who stopped hiding what she felt. And Yusuf, who is about to discover that being admired can be its own kind of trap.
screen: `A BANQUET, AND A KNIFE EACH.` · `THIS IS NO HUMAN BEING.` · `THE QUR'AN NEVER SAYS FRUIT.` · `HALF OF ALL BEAUTY.` · then, large: `BEAUTY IS A TEST TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how people react to beauty. Settle, and breathe. Think of the last time you saw someone or something striking: a face, a sunset, a perfect car. What happened in you? Attraction, envy, the urge to take a photo, to own it, to compare yourself? Let the reaction come back and look at it with curiosity, not shame. Then think of how people react to your own looks, or to how you'd like to look. Does it make you anxious, proud, invisible? If you pray, you can ask for eyes that see beauty without being ruled by it. The bell holds the time.
The knives and the fruit. A dinner party, a knife in every hand, and a young man so striking that the guests cut themselves. Today's word.
screen: `THE KNIVES AND THE FRUIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: beauty is a test too. Today, when something beautiful catches your eye, notice what it asks of you before you answer. Day sixty-two.

63.title: Prison, chosen
63.hook: Yusuf prays that prison is dearer to him than what they ask of him
63.howItsDone: Muslims honor Yusuf's choice of prison as a model of chastity and integrity, often alongside the hadith of the seven whom Allah shades, which includes one who refuses a woman of rank and beauty, saying "I fear Allah."

screen: `DAY SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the knives and the fruit, a banquet where beauty tested everyone. Your line was beauty is a test too. What did beauty ask of you? Day sixty-three, the end of the week.
screen: `BEAUTY IS A TEST TOO.`

segments.voice: Most of us have faced a choice between the comfortable wrong thing and the uncomfortable right one. Keep quiet and keep the job, or speak up and lose it. Go along with the group, or walk home alone. Usually the price is a bad week, an awkward dinner. After the banquet, the pressure on Yusuf isn't coming from one woman anymore. The wife has said it in front of everyone: if he doesn't do what I tell him, he'll be imprisoned, and humiliated. And the Qur'an suggests the others are pressing him too. He's cornered, in a comfortable house. And he turns and prays. Today: prison, chosen.
screen: `THE COMFORTABLE WRONG THING.` → `DO IT, OR PRISON.` → `CORNERED IN A GOOD HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse thirty-three. He says: my Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they're calling me to. And unless You turn their scheming away from me, I'll lean toward them, and be one of the ignorant. Two things in that prayer. First, the choice itself. He isn't sentenced yet. He's asking for the cell over the palace. Prison, the Arabic sijn, the place of walls and locks, is dearer to him, more beloved, than the easy life with a compromise at the center. He'd rather lose his freedom than lose himself. Second, look how honest he is. He doesn't say, don't worry, I'm strong. He says: unless You help me, I'll slip. Remember his cry in the house of the Aziz, I seek refuge in Allah. Same man, same humility. He knows the pull is real. And the next verse: so his Lord answered him, and turned their scheming away. Then, even after they'd seen all the signs of his innocence, the verse says it seemed best to them to imprison him for a time. The innocent man goes to prison, and the story doesn't pretend that's fair. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a hadith in Bukhari, named among the seven people Allah shades on the Day when there's no shade but His: a man called by a woman of rank and beauty, who says, I fear Allah. And that's the week. A boy in a well. A father's beautiful patience. Sold for coins. A house with closed doors. A torn shirt. A banquet. And now a cell, chosen.
screen: `PRISON IS DEARER TO ME.` · `UNLESS YOU TURN IT FROM ME.` · `HIS LORD ANSWERED HIM.` · `IMPRISONED ANYWAY, FOR A TIME.` · then, large: `THE PRISON WAS FREER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the harder right thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life where the easy option and the right option have split apart. Maybe small: telling the cashier they undercharged you, admitting the mistake before anyone finds it, skipping the gossip. Picture both roads. Feel the comfort of the easy one. Then picture yourself choosing the other, and notice: what's the prison you're afraid of? Is it really so bad? If you pray, you can use Yusuf's honesty: unless You help me, I'll slip. The bell holds the time.
Prison. The cell Yusuf chose over a comfortable compromise, and asked for help to keep choosing. Today's word.
screen: `PRISON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the prison was freer. Once today, choose the harder right thing, and notice whether it leaves you lighter. Day sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 63 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO DREAMS IN A CELL.`
